claims.text: The starting additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has a relatively uniform elemental distribution and no pronounced pre-existing oxide scale.
Grain boundaries provide fast diffusion paths for Al and Ti during elevated-temperature exposure.
Under oxidizing conditions, grain-boundary diffusion of Al and Ti produces continuous, band-like Al2O3 and TiO2 scales along grain boundaries.
Continuous Al- or Ti-containing oxide scales are initially protective against further oxidation.
The proposed oxide scales eventually become brittle and crack because of growth stresses and interfacial decohesion.
Cracking of the grain-boundary oxide scales promotes intergranular cracking, embrittlement, and loss of tensile ductility.
An H2-rich reducing atmosphere provides insufficient oxygen for substantial formation of the proposed grain-boundary oxides.
Suppressing oxide formation under reducing conditions preserves intergranular integrity and bulk mechanical properties.
Oxidizing exposure will produce thicker and more continuous grain-boundary oxides, more microcracking, and lower tensile elongation than either the reducing exposure or the as-fabricated baseline.
Reducing-atmosphere samples will show minimal oxidation and retain mechanical properties close to the as-fabricated baseline.
The proposed governing mechanism applies over 700–900 °C and exposure durations of approximately 1–24 hours.
Much higher temperatures or substantially longer exposures may introduce phase transformations or additional oxidation mechanisms.
The additively manufactured microstructure contains an abundance of grain boundaries that promotes short-circuit diffusion.
Oxidizing and reducing exposures should use identically processed samples and identical thermal histories, differing only in gas atmosphere.
SEM, EDS, and TEM measurements of oxide continuity and thickness, crack density, and mechanical testing can distinguish the proposed mechanism.

The hypothesis is falsified if oxidizing exposure causes no statistically significant increase in continuous grain-boundary oxides and associated cracking or mechanical degradation relative to both reducing exposure and the baseline.
